title: Rolf de Heer Named President of Tokyo Film Festival Jury
description: The Tokyo International Film Festival has named Australian director Rolf de Heer president of the international competition jury for the festival’s
body:
The Tokyo International Film Festival has named Australian director Rolf de Heer president of the international competition jury for the festival’s 39th edition.

	De Heer has spent more than 40 years in Tasmania, Australia, directing, writing and producing films across a broad range of genres and subjects. His 1993 feature “Bad Boy Bubby” won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival, along with the festival’s Fipresci Prize. Four of his films have made the official selection at Cannes, among them “Ten Canoes” (2006), winner of the Special Jury Prize in the Un Certain Regard section.
	

	This year’s World Focus lineup at TIFF will include Australia Spotlight, a dedicated showcase of Australian cinema mounted with the Australian Embassy in Japan. The series will screen de Heer’s “The Survival of Kindness” (2022), a competition entry at the 73rd Berlin Film Festival that went on to win the Fipresci Prize there.


	“For any of us attending the Tokyo International Film Festival, it is a privilege,” de Heer said. “For me, as a filmmaker, it is even more so. The more films I manage to make, the fewer films I manage to see, especially on the big screen. But as a part of this jury, I have the duty, the obligation, to see at least 15 films and talk about them with other filmmakers.”

	Hisamatsu Takeo, festival director of TIFF, said he was delighted to welcome de Heer as jury president. “With his distinctive perspective and unwavering commitment to filmmaking, de Heer has spent decades opening up new possibilities in cinema,” Hisamatsu said. “We look forward to the fresh dialogue and discoveries that his wealth of experience and deep insight will bring to this year’s Competition and its diverse selection of films.”
	

	De Heer trained at the Australian Film, Television and Radio School and has since written or co-written 14 screenplays that reached the screen as feature films. His director’s credits run to 15 and a half features spanning a range of budgets and genres, and he has produced or co-produced 16 fiction films and five documentaries.

	Career highlights include “Dingo” (1991), starring Colin Friels and jazz musician Miles Davis; “The Tracker” (2002), which began de Heer’s collaborations with Australian Aboriginal actor David Gulpilil; and “Charlie’s Country” (2013), for which Gulpilil won the best actor award at Cannes. “Alexandra’s Project” (2003) earned Helen Buday a best actress award at the San Sebastian Film Festival after the film screened in competition at the Berlin Film Festival.

	The 39th TIFF will run Oct. 26-Nov. 4. TIFFCOM, the festival’s industry market, will take place Oct. 28-30.

schema.headline: Rolf de Heer Named President of Tokyo Film Festival Jury

title: ‘Gremlins 3’ Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros.
description:
Warner Bros. has delayed “Gremlins 3” from Nov. 19, 2027, to Oct. 6. 2028.

	David Zaslav, the CEO and president of Warner Bros. Discovery, first re
body:
Warner Bros. has delayed “Gremlins 3” from Nov. 19, 2027, to Oct. 6. 2028.

	David Zaslav, the CEO and president of Warner Bros. Discovery, first revealed the project during an investor call in 2025. Steven Spielberg is returning as executive producer alongside Maiden Voyage’s Eleanor Columbus. “Harry Potter” filmmaker Chris Columbus is set to produce and direct. Hannah Marks is writing the script from an original draft by Chris Columbus, Zach Lipovsky and Adam Stein.
	

	Kristie Macosko Krieger and Holly Bario are producing under Amblin Entertainment alongside Michael Barnathan and Mark Radcliffe of 26th Street Pictures. The official title, plot details and casting have not been disclosed.


	Joe Dante’s original 1984 “Gremlins,” which played a role in creating the PG-13 film rating, was a horror comedy following a young boy named Billy who receives a cute, furry yet mysterious creature called a Mogwai. The two become fast friends, but Billy’s new pet comes with two strict rules: Never get the Mogwai wet and never feed it after midnight. Of course, those regulations are broken. The gremlin then multiplies and creates chaos in Billy’s small town during the holiday season.

	The first “Gremlins” was a box office smash, grossing $212 million worldwide against a budget of about $11 million. The 1990 follow-up, “Gremlins 2: The New Batch,” only mustered $41 million by the end of its run but is considered a cult classic.

	“Few titles are as beloved and iconic as ‘Gremlins,’ and we’re beyond excited to bring it back for both lifelong fans and a whole new generation,” Warner Bros. Pictures’ president of development and production Jesse Ehrman said in a statement at the time of the announcement of “Gremlins 3.” “It’s a privilege to be working alongside Steven [Spielberg], Chris [Columbus], and the entire creative team, and we look forward to audiences experiencing the next installment of the magic, mayhem and heart of Gremlins on the big screen in 2027.”

title: Barry Diller Drops Bid to Acquire MGM Resorts: ‘We Didn’t Feel the Mix Was Coming Together’
description:
People Inc., the media company controlled by Barry Diller, is scrapping its proposed bid to acquire MGM Resorts International.

	People Inc. (which
body:
People Inc., the media company controlled by Barry Diller, is scrapping its proposed bid to acquire MGM Resorts International.

	People Inc. (which changed its name from IAC this spring) owns about 27% of MGM Resorts. In June, the company submitted formal offer for the hotel and online-gaming operator to acquire all outstanding shares of MGM that People Inc. did not already own for $48.30 per share in cash. The bid valued MGM Resorts at around $18 billion.
	

	But on Wednesday, People Inc. said it was withdrawing the offer.


	Diller, who serves as People Inc.’s chairman and senior executive, said in a statement, “There are lots of ingredients that go into a proposal of this kind on its way to completion. We didn’t feel the mix was coming together in the way we had hoped and have decided not to pursue taking the company private at this time.”

	Diller added, “What is undimmed is our belief in the future of MGM Resorts. We continue to hold 66.8 million shares representing approximately 27% of MGM Resorts and have total confidence in both the management and the Company’s prospects.”

	The media mogul added, “People Incorporated is doing just fine with its principal publishing business achieving its 11th quarter of growth with plenty of cash to both invest in its business and purchase its stock.”

	People Inc. remains “open to and interested in the possibility of a strategic transaction with MGM Resorts and look forward to considering a range of alternatives,” Diller said.

	MGM Resorts on Wednesday confirmed People Inc.’s move to drop the takeover bid.
	

	“The board remains excited to continue to lead MGM Resorts as a standalone company. Our leading position in Las Vegas, our best-in-class regional properties, and BetMGM’s continued momentum highlight the value we bring to our shareholders,” MGM Resorts chairman Paul Salem said in a statement.

	MGM Resorts operates 30 hotel and casino destinations globally and owns 50% of BetMGM, a sports betting and online gaming platform, in a joint venture with U.K. gambling operator Entain. The company is currently “pursuing targeted expansion in Asia” through an integrated resort development in Japan.

	Back in June, Diller had said MGM Resorts “represented a rare kind of business: one with real-world assets that AI cannot easily replicate or disintermediate and exceptional digital growth opportunities.”

	Diller — who once run Paramount Pictures and tried to acquire Paramount before Viacom’s Sumner Redstone outbid him — originally formed Silver King Broadcasting in 1996 as a media holding company and change its name to IAC (InterActiveCorp) in 2004. The company’s Dotdash Meredith publishing unit in July 2025 had changed its name to People Inc., and Diller subsequently decided to apply that name to the whole enterprise.

	IAC over the years owned and operated more than 200 companies and overseen over 100 minority investments. It has spun off 11 businesses including Match Group, Expedia, LendingTree, HSN (now part of QVC Group, which recently filed for bankruptcy), Ticketmaster (now part of Live Nation Entertainment) and Angi.

	In late 2021, IAC acquired Meredith in a $2.7 billion deal, three years after Meredith bought Time Inc. (and following Meredith’s sale of titles including Time, now owned by Salesforce’s Marc Benioff; Fortune; and Sports Illustrated). Today, People Inc.’s 40-plus brands include People, Food + Wine, Southern Living, Travel & Leisure, Allrecipes, Better Homes & Gardens, InStyle, Verywell, Investopedia and EW.

title: ‘Game Changer’ Host Sam Reich on Season 8’s 23-Contestant, 90-Minute, Non-Chili’s-Sponsored Finale and ‘Acid Trip’ Season 9 Episode Plans
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 8 finale of “Game Changer,” now streaming on Dropout.

	“Game Changer” capped off its e
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 8 finale of “Game Changer,” now streaming on Dropout.

	“Game Changer” capped off its eighth season Monday with a finale episode that was not at all sponsored by Chili’s but ended with its winner taking home between $3,000 and $5,000 (host and Dropout CEO Sam Reich isn’t sure) in Chili’s gift cards. Combine that with the fact the Season 8 finale (a talent show competition) is the longest episode of the Dropout series to date (coming in at just under 90 minutes) and boasts the largest number of contestants (23) and you’ve got a wildly unprecedented undertaking for Reich and the “Game Changer” team.
	

	The episode, titled “Last Talent Standing,” features nearly two dozen contestants performing in a talent show with a “Squid Game”-esque twist that “killed off” eliminated competitors who then joined a panel of judges led by guest stars Kumail Nanjiani, Maria Bamford and Gianmarco Soresi. 


	“What you see in this 90-minute episode is extraordinarily faithful to everything that actually occurred,” Reich tells Variety. “There is not a single go that we lifted out of the show completely.”

	(It should be noted the episode does cut Katie Marovitch’s answer to the way she’d like to fake die upon her elimination, which was deemed “too dark” for Dropout’s standards. “Yeah, I think Katie and I will probably take that one to the grave, so to speak,” Reich says.)

	Reich was willing to let the cameras roll indefinitely to capture the seemingly endless talents (from Japanese fan dancing to mind reading) of the Dropout players. But what he wasn’t up for was making another two-part episode.
	

	“Most ‘Game Changer’ shoots go as long as they need to,” Reich says. “The difference between this season and prior seasons is, if you’re looking for how we’ve creatively pivoted, we’ve done episodes that we’ve split in two. Many. In fact, if you look at other two-parters, the sum of their parts is not as long as this 90 minutes was. I have finally landed against two-parters, and the reason is that I feel like we set up expectations and then there’s no way to surprise people as much with the second half. So their experience of watching an episode, waiting a week — actually two weeks — and then watching the second half is always going to be a funny kind of payoff where that second half better be, in some ways, profoundly different from the first half in order to still feel like ‘Game Changer.’ And I would rather wallop people with one experience. So now that we can afford to, that’s basically what this comes down to. We’re just doing longer episodes here and there.”

	Though Reich says he’s done breaking episodes into two parts, there is still a limit to how long he’s willing to let an episode go based on his initial plans in a writers’ room vs. what happens during the actual production.

	“There were game mechanics that we had to abandon because the day was immediately running so long and the biggest game mechanic that we had to abandon was mini games that were going to happen in between rounds and those mini games were going to be all players squaring off in the same talent,” Reich says. “For instance, we were going to reach the end of round one and then the players were going to go heads up on beatboxing or heads up on best Scottish accent or heads up on runway walk — which Oscar did do for us later in the episode — and we were quickly running so, so long that was not possible. Winners of those games were going to get a ‘one free death’ or ‘resurrection’ certificate. Our thinking was they could use them on themselves or they could unselfishly use them on someone else, which might also create a funny dynamic.”

	Reich says that those planned aspects had to be cut out to account for the lengthy production day, but there was a key mechanic he made sure could stay in no matter how long the episode got.

	“There is a distinction between what I am willing to do and what, like a ‘Squid Game’ or a ‘Beast Games’ is willing to do and part of that for me at this point is trying to figure out, if I’m going to do an elimination game, ways that eliminated players are going to stay involved,” Reich says. “So turning eliminated players into judges was important to me for that reason.”
	

	Once the game got down to its final four contestants — Jacob Wysocki, Kimia Behpoornia, Kaylin Mahoney and Oscar Montoya — Reich says the competition hit its “tipping point,” as the desire to end the very long production day and go home warred with everyone’s goal to commit to the bit. This led to moments like Wysocki trying and failing to eliminate himself to, as he (the only “straight white guy” left at that point) put it, “give voices to people who matter” and so he could “go smoke a joint in my car.”

	“The meta game of ‘Game Changer’ at any point is that probably everyone is just trying to create the best possible episode, regardless of if that means they’re winning,” Reich says. “I think everyone’s sort of producer brain is — meaning all of my players, and this is what makes for such a good show — probably a little higher than their game-player brain. Not all the time, but sometimes. Which means that I can count on players doing the funny thing, even if that means getting eliminated. Jacob, I think he was sort of saying to himself, ‘I don’t need to win this. The day is already going long. I want for one of my friends to win it,’ and just no one would allow it. And that was, in some ways, the tipping point of the episode, where we went from running long to that being the spirit of the day. To everyone wanting to hang in there as long as possible.”

	Ultimately, Montoya walked away the proud owner of a Chili’s gift card with “under $5,000″ on it, courtesy of Dropout, not Chili’s — though that was not for lack of Reich trying to get Chili’s involved.

	“I absolutely did,” Reich says. “Granted, I could have probably pressed on that more than I did. There was something about the fact that all of that happened and we weren’t sponsored by anybody, which is also funny. Just like if this ends up being the result, it’s just the result.”

	As Dropout has grown, the company has set a steady pace with production and release cycles for its expanding slate of TV shows, which also includes “Dimension 20,” “Make Some Noise” and “Very Important People.” That means that even though “Game Changer” Season 8 has just concluded for viewers, the episodes were shot so long ago now that Reich’s focus has shifted to the ninth season, which begins production in three weeks. And he is trying to limit how the response to Season 8 affects new ideas.
	

	“I’m so deeply entrenched in Season 9 that even to turn back and reflect on it, it’s tricky,” Reich says. “It requires me extracting my brain from one Frankenstein and putting it in another Frankenstein. There’s a natural sort of built-in tweak to ‘Game Changer,’ which is the show itself is such an experiment and we’re lucky to have fans who really care about it. But for the most part, I try to tune out the noise and to remain faithful to the experiment. And what to me that means is every season, it is a show that, like a cat, will always be exploring the perimeter of what it can do because it’s always looking for new things to exploit. And because the show gets bigger and bigger, there’s more at its disposal to be able to exploit season after season. So every season we have this conversation with ourselves, which is sort of like, what do we want to see a little bit more of? What do we want to see a little bit less of? And in some ways, every season is a response to the season that came before it.”

	The focus between Seasons 7 and 8 was pushing the boundaries for game design, and Reich says he’s “really proud of what we came up with” for Season 8’s episodes, which has “some of the truest games that we’ve ever done with the show.”

	Now going into Season 9, Reich says these episodes are planned to be “by a mile, the strangest stuff we’ve ever done.” 

	“It is just like whatever those game design impulses were [for Season 8], [Season 9] hasn’t left them entirely in the gutter, but it is like an acid trip,” Reich says. “The show benefits not at all from consistency. So we’ll continue to reinvent it, and it’ll continue to shape-shift and that’s part of the fun of being on this ride.”

schema.headline: ‘Game Changer’ Host Sam Reich on Season 8’s 23-Contestant, 90-Minute, Non-Chili’s-Sponsored Finale and ‘Acid Trip’ Season 9 Episode Plans

title: Roseanne Barr Rages Against Ex Co-Star Michael Fishman for Saying ‘Roseanne’ Reboot Was ‘Rightfully Canceled’: ‘You F—ing Little Worm’ and ‘Brainwashed Bigot’
description: Roseanne Barr and her original “Roseanne” co-star Michael Fishman are still feuding over the cancellation of the show’s 2018 reboot. Fishman made he
body:
Roseanne Barr and her original “Roseanne” co-star Michael Fishman are still feuding over the cancellation of the show’s 2018 reboot. Fishman made headlines in August for saying “the show was rightfully canceled” after Barr posted a tweet that appeared to link Barack Obama’s advisor Valerie Jarrett, who is Black, to “Planet of the Apes.” Barr was accused of being racist but has long maintained that was not her intention. 

	During a new interview on the “Can’t Be Censored” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly), Barr was asked to weigh in on Fishman’s comments supporting ABC’s decision to pull the 2018 “Roseanne” reboot. She did so by unleashing a tirade against her former co-star.
	

	“He fucking doesn’t even fucking know what I said, even though I’ve explained it 10,000 times for nine years on the Internet,” Barr said. “He hasn’t even taken the time to listen to what I say because he’s a bigot. And he’s a brainwashed bigot.”

	Barr claimed that Fishman once asked her to clarify her controversial tweet that got the reboot canceled, to which she told him: “Let me explain this, Michael, go and fuck yourself and stay fucked ‘till the day you die. Don’t put my name in your fucking mouth; shut the fuck up. You are an ignoramus and a bigot, and you have no idea what I said because it contradicts the Democratic Party platform that you’ve had shoved down your throat and up your ass. So just fuck you. You have no geopolitical context whatsoever to discuss what I said.”

	“Roseanne” was canceled after Barr tweeted: “muslim brotherhood & planet of the apes had a baby=vj.” The tweet was widely perceived as a racist insult toward Valerie Jarrett, although Barr claims otherwise. She stressed in her new interview that she was evoking the 2015 Iran nuclear deal and that “Planet of the Apes” is a nickname she used to describe the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
	

	“You think I said Black people look like monkeys,” Barr continued in her lashing out at Fishman. “Go fuck yourself, you little fucking worm. And I’m glad they fired you because I was the only reason you were ever on that show. They wanted to get rid of you in the reboot and I made them take you back.”

	Barr is referring to Fishman’s abrupt exit from “The Conners,” the ABC sitcom that continued the “Roseanne” franchise sans Barr following the reboot’s cancellation. “The Conners” ran for seven seasons, with Fishman reprising D.J. Conner for four seasons before revealing in 2022 that “I was told I would not be returning for season 5.” It’s never been confirmed why ABC dropped him.

	Fishman has always opposed Barr’s tweet. He “vehemently” condemned the post after the “Roseanne” reboot was canceled and called his co-stars’ comments “reprehensible and intolerable.” She fired back at the time by posting: “You throw me under the bus.”

	In a video posted to his Instagram in August, Fishman spoke out against claims that it was “woke crap” that got the “Roseanne” reboot canceled.

	“I get these kinds of ignorant and inaccurate comments daily,” Fishman said. “After eight years, turning the other cheek is really not helping. So, I guess the world failed to learn the lesson, so I’m going to point out — we are perpetuating a lie, and people are using a political smokescreen to justify the indefensible… Those justifications, they’re leading to real consequences, real crimes, situations like Trey Reed and Tasha Fortune, because dehumanizing people is never a joke.”

	Fishman acknowledged that comedians can make people laugh at the “darkest” of topics, but “sadly, in this case, there was no joke. And the show was rightfully canceled.”

schema.headline: Roseanne Barr Rages Against Ex Co-Star Michael Fishman for Saying ‘Roseanne’ Reboot Was ‘Rightfully Canceled’: ‘You F—ing Little Worm’ and ‘Brainwashed Bigot’

title: Jeff Garlin Says ‘Undiagnosed Bipolar’ Made Him ‘Mean’ on ‘The Goldbergs’ Set; Wendi McLendon-Covey Responds: ‘I Remember Things Differently’
description: Jeff Garlin revealed in a recent interview on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly) that he had undiagnosed bipolar disord
body:
Jeff Garlin revealed in a recent interview on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly) that he had undiagnosed bipolar disorder during the making of ABC’s “The Goldbergs,” which he notably exited from after an HR investigation into multiple claims of inappropriate conduct against him. The 1980s-set family sitcom, which ran for 10 seasons and 229 episodes from 2013 to 2023, starred Garlin opposite Wendi McLendon-Covey. Garlin exited in 2021.
	

	“At the time, I was undiagnosed bipolar,” Garlin said on the podcast, noting he got his diagnosis after exiting the series. “I was miserable on the show, and I was miserable with my performance. And [Wendi] was always trying to tell me, ‘Hey, you’re really great on the show.’ I didn’t believe her. I just got to the point where I had to quit, and she was very resentful.”


	Garlin added, “Being bipolar, I was either one of three things: dark, dark, dark, dark, didn’t talk and look at anyone; happy to the point of mania, never turning off my thing; or mean — really, really mean.” 

	McLendon-Covey reacted to Garlin’s comments on Instagram by disputing his comments: “Huh. Let’s just say I remember things very differently, as does the crew, the other actors, the writers, and our executives.”

	When Garlin exited “The Goldbergs” in 2021, two sources close to the production confirmed to Variety that it was a mutual decision between the actor and the network. Shortly before, Garlin addressed allegations against him in an interview with Vanity Fair, acknowledging that an HR investigation into his on-set behavior had been ongoing for the past three years and dismissing a rumor that he had been fired from the series.
	

	“We have a difference of opinion, Sony and myself. Okay. My opinion is, I have my process about how I’m funny, in terms of the scene and what I have to do. They feel that it makes for a quote ‘unsafe’ workspace,” Garlin said at the time. “Now, mind you, my silliness making an unsafe workspace — I don’t understand how that is… I am always a kind and thoughtful person. I make mistakes, sure. But my comedy is about easing people’s pain. Why would I ever want to cause pain in anybody for a laugh? That’s bullying. That’s just uncalled for.”

	The allegations against Garlin ranged from unwanted hugging and touching people on set to telling jokes that made others uncomfortable. McLendon-Covey later said during an interview with Andy Cohen for SiriusXM that Garlin’s exit was “a long time coming.”

	“That it finally happened, it was like, ‘Ok, finally someone is listening to us.’ But that was kind of hard though because we had lost George Segal in real life,” she added. “To have to go through another loss on a sitcom…you can’t keep asking your audience to mourn people. That’s not why they tune in… I’m exhausted by that topic and the PTSD of it all. I just feel like the less people know about that, the better. No one benefits from knowing anything.”

	“The Goldbergs” was in the middle of filming its ninth season when Garlin was fired. As Variety exclusively reported at the time, producers decided to keep Garlin’s character on the show for the rest of the season by using off-camera dialogue and unused takes pulled from earlier episodes, as well as previously shot images of Garlin. The actor’s stand-in was also used in group scenes, but he was shot from the back. The final result was visually awkward and earned so many complaints on social media that McLendon-Covey even weighed in at the time.

	“This season threw us for a loop because it’s hard to incorporate someone who doesn’t want to be there and wants to leave mid-scene, and we weren’t about to rewrite the second half of the season,” the comedian wrote on Twitter at the time. “We’re doing our best.”

	When “The Goldbergs” kicked off its 10th and final season last fall, the show killed off Garlin’s character.

schema.headline: Jeff Garlin Says ‘Undiagnosed Bipolar’ Made Him ‘Mean’ on ‘The Goldbergs’ Set; Wendi McLendon-Covey Responds: ‘I Remember Things Differently’

title: ‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse Review: The ’50s Absurdist Comedy Is Too Smug in Its Peak-Bleak View of Venal Humanity, but Jefferson Mays and Melinda Page Hamilton Are Worth the Visit
description: When an “Amadeus” revival opened at Pasadena Playhouse in February, it was such a spectacular success on every level that you wouldn’t have minded i
body:
When an “Amadeus” revival opened at Pasadena Playhouse in February, it was such a spectacular success on every level that you wouldn’t have minded if the keepers of the venerable San Gabriel Valley venue just turned over the keys to the place for a while to the two Tony winners most responsible for making it a smash: star Jefferson Mays and director Darko Tresnjak. And that’s kind of what the Playhouse has done. That dynamic duo is already back in Pasadena with “The Visit,” which has opened a mere seven months after “Amadeus” first hit the boards there. With a good number of cast and crew members carrying over from the previous production to rock us again after “Amadeus,” this looks, for the moment, like as close a thing to an official house company as you can get in a major theater nowadays.
	

	But is “The Visit” as much fun as “Amadeus”? Let’s just say for the moment that this followup production is destined to be more polarizing than that across-the-board crowd pleaser, although it’s not even a bit less lively. Like Peter Shaffer’s play before it, it is a vintage black comedy — even more vintage, as it was written by Swiss playwright Friedrich Dürrenmatt in 1956, although it’s been subject to a lot of Engligh adaptations and re-writes in subsequent decades. It loosely belongs to the theater of absurdism, which means that there is increasing room as the tragicomedy proceeds for Tresnjak to play around with the initially realistic trappings and have some fun with surrealist, grotesque and/or anachronistic elements. But what it really belongs to is the theater of fatalism, where things line up along the way to increasingly convince us that society, government and individua people themselves are inevitably subject to corruption and venality. So your enjoyment of the play may finally be subject to how much you feel you already do or don’t know that.
	

	Given that Mays is widely regarded as one of the most charismatic and capable actors in modern theater, would it surprise you to learn that he is not really the star of “The Visit”? Well, he is, certainly in billing, and in the fact that he is the clear protagonist, as Anton Schill, a humble shopkeeper in postwar (or is it 2020s?) Europe whose past comes back to haunt him. But Mays is playing almost more of a mouse than a man. So, talk about a turnaround from Salieri. As much scenery-chewing as the actor was doing in “Amadeus” — and it was a glorious meal — that’s how little he’s doing here. Mays admitted in a recent interview that he wasn’t sure he was right for the role, and you can see why he might have thought so, given the character’s passivity. But it takes a skilled actor to successfully put his mojo on mute, too. So if you know what he’s capable of, there’s some pleasure in watching him at first seem to embody the milk of human kindness, before he succumbs more of an emblem ofBut the the milquetoast of human depravity.



	

					Melinda Page Hamilton in ‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse
									Jeff Lorch/Pasadena Playhouse
	



	But the obvious centrifugal force of “The Visit” is the female lead, a character named Claire Zachanassian who may be the richest woman in the world, and who has an even greater surfeit of personality than money. She’s played here to perfection by Melinda Page Hamilton, whose stage appearances and recurring TV roles have not made her a household name — yet she has such presence that, from her first scene forward, you’re convinced that she must be one anyway. She gets off a train and breezes into the downtrodden European town where she spent her impoverished girlhood like she is some charming ane cunning combination of Lauren Bacall, Madonna and a demonically possessed Daisy Buchanan. Her intentions for the hometown she is nostalgically revisiting are cloaked at first, but her barbed banter is so much fun, you can almost half-wish she doesn’t mean anything sinister with her visit, even if she clearly does. After all, her musclebound handlers have brought along with them an empty casket, and this is the sort of play where a coffin that appears in the first act is definitely going to go off in the third. (Not literally; although “The Visit” has been produced in as a hefty three-parter in some productions, it’s mercifully cut down to a single act in Pasadena.) You can never take your eyes or ears off Hamilton, even when the plot gives her increasingly schematic things to say and do in the second half.
	

	About that plot. There is a big revelation less than halfway into the show, one that might even count as a plot twist, and thus something not to be spoiled… if not for the fact that virtually every synopsis in the last 70 years has included it in the first sentence. So we’ll assume most patrons know it going in and won’t hold a discussion of it against us here, though stop right now if you think you might. Cutting to the chase, Claire has earmarked the aforementioned casket for Anton, despite the fact that he was her lover in their youthful days, and they are sharing sweet memories of their lusty romps in the woods within minutes of her arrival. After some more talk of the bucolic days gone by, Claire suddenly announces at a town meeting that she will rescue this on-the-skids burg with a donation of one billion (what the currency is goes unspecified), with one condition: that they deliver her a dead Anton. For reasons eventually to be revealed, she represents pure vengeance, even if she does talk like someone out of a ’30s screwball comedy, or “Truth or Dare.”

	Up to the point that she delivers the townspeople this ultimatum — a deal with the devil, or with an especially cocktail-party-friendly Cruella de Vil — “The Visit” has kind of been a rollicking good time. For much of the audience, it will remain that all the way to the end, even with some somber moments along the way that aren’t played for laughs. But the basic problem with the play — if you’re spoilsport enough to see it as one — is that once Claire makes her modest proposal to save the town, there won’t likely be any doubt in a single audience member’s mind that things are going to pan out exactly as she wants them to. Because it’s that kind of a show: one that is just a little too self-pleased with itself for offering the bleakest possible vision of what civilized people can and probably will do, offered a way out of their misery or mundanity. So there’s not that much to happen in the last two-thirds of the drama than for your ribs to be constantly nudged with the idea of how easily the most respectable citizens among us will give in to modest proposals and, indeed, murder. It rings true, don’t get me wrong! But it also rings awfully predictable, in a way that maybe it didn’t in the late ’50s and ’60s, when it was a little easier for defiantly grim morality tales to seem transgressive in the mainstream.
	



	

					‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse
									Jeff Lorch/Pasadena Playhouse
	



	The story might have at least a modicum of suspense if any of the upstanding townspeople were seen as struggling with the idea of murdering a trusted friend. But after an initial vote of “no way” to Claire’s offer, everyone seems to have become completely transformed by the next morning. The program notes reference “Invasion of the Body Snatchers,” which seems like an apt analogy, except that that film would be a lot less riveting if the entire city turned into pod people instantly, followed by an hour of Kevin McCarthy slowly deciding he should accept his fate. To give some credit here, there is one scene in which a cleric openly debates with himself whether to go along with the greedy mob or not, but within a couple of minutes he’s come to terms with the creeping evil, too. It’s realistic, sad to say, that a population would find a way to justify throw all of its collective principles away and commit a horrific crime; it’s just a little less realistic — or good for the purposes of a full-length drama — that this would all happen in a virtual instant.

	There are other huge dramatic implausibilities, if we want to get picky about it. The opening scenes of “The Visit,” when it is in its most realistic mode, have the townspeople convinced that Anton is actually their ticket to riches, not a future scapegoat, because of his past romance with Claire. And he seems to be firmly convinced of this, too, as they get together alone in the woods and share reminiscings of those tender or erotic moments of yore. But once Claire reveals the backstory of why she is out to bring the wrath of God down on him, her reasoning seems… well, still a little psychopathic, but somewhat justified, by the standard of modern feminist morality tales. To say he did her wrong is an understatement. So is Anton supposed to be mentally compromised or deranged, rather than the harmless soul we first meet him as, to have imagined that Claire would have come back after all these decades with a positive picture of him, instead of a lust for blood? It makes no sense. Maybe that’s a fault of the condensation, and the picture would be clearer in the three-and-a-half-hour version (!) Tony Kushner adapted for the London stage at the turn of the decade. But there’s some basic sense missing here that can’t be explained away with the idea that it’s just a surrealist fable.
	

	With all that said, there are still a lot of pleasures in this production that remain failsafe, even after the ride toward a way-too-inevitable outcome is firmly on its tracks. For instance, the way that Tresnjak, wardrobe designer Charlotte DeVaux Shields and set designer Alexander Dodge have conspired to make sneakers into the embodiment of complicity and evil is fairly ingenious. Somehow, the show’s supporting cast members manage to make their way onstage without giving away their footwear until, at some key moment, their colorful shoes are lit up in what looks like a flurorescent glow, revealing that they, too, have gone along with the body snatchers. (Everyone should see it coming a mile away, but even I LOL-ed when the town cleric showed that he, also, has succumbed to the Air Jordan pandemic.) There are an increasing number of moments like that throughout the production in which it seems to have suddenly jumped into the present day, and some work, some don’t. It is a little jarring when, still pretty early in the show, you hear the first example of disco bumper music, like they suddenly piped in a little bit of David Byrne’s score for “Here Lies Love” to cover the scene change. But by the end, the use of modern-day cameras and video screens to bring the action fully into the 2020s seems justified enough, if you buy into Tresnjak’s time-tripping aesthetic at all.



	

					‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse
									Jeff Lorch/Pasadena Playhouse
	



	The show’s creepiest characters — no contest here — are a couple of aging, balding, blind eunuchs (played by Jake Levy and Lauren Worsham)who seem to be part of Claire’s entourage for no good reason, other than to figure into the tale of woe she eventually tells, which finally explains why they know their way around the town so well despite being sightless visitors. Their presence brings “The Visit” almost right up to the edge of horror, which is where thematically it kind of belongs, despite all the zingers, smirks and guffaws. The play seems to want to flirt with the idea of Grand Guignol, even if remains more firmly rooted in the land of Samuel Beckett.

	But the swing being taken here is bold enough that there’s no reason to want to take the Playhouse keys back from Tresnjak, if he has more offbeat revival aspirations where this one came from. And with lead performances like Mays’ and Hamilton’s, the production is — sorry to do this here — worth your visit. If the initial impulse is that Mays doesn’t have as much to do here as is worthy of his talent, he is so firmly enmeshed in the character of a nebbish caught up in a sub-Kafkaesque nightmare, he makes you feel deeply for his fate, even if Maurice Valency’s adapted script kind of seems to want you to not feel so bad about it. And Melinda Page Hamilton? She’s so captivating, in both her rages and her funnier, more casual cruelty, that I’d follow her Claire to just about any soiree where the multi-billionaire elite meet, even if I did spot a coffin there with my name on it.
	

	“The Visit” runs through Oct. 4 at Pasadena Playhouse, located at 39 South El Molino Ave. in Pasadena. Phone: 626-356-7529. For tickets and more information, visit http://www.pasadenaplayhouse.org.

schema.headline: ‘The Visit’ at Pasadena Playhouse Review: The ’50s Absurdist Comedy Is Too Smug in Its Peak-Bleak View of Venal Humanity, but Jefferson Mays and Melinda Page Hamilton Are Worth the Visit

title: Original ‘Willy Wonka’ Oompa-Loompa Rusty Goffe ‘Shed a Tear’ at Gene Wilder’s Voice Recreated by AI: ‘It Was Lovely Hearing It Again’
description: “Have a scrumdiddlyumptious day!” is how Rusty Goffe, who played an Oompa-Loompa in the 1971 adaptation of “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” opp
body:
“Have a scrumdiddlyumptious day!” is how Rusty Goffe, who played an Oompa-Loompa in the 1971 adaptation of “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” opposite Gene Wilder, signs off our Zoom call after we speak earlier this month.

	With such Wonka-isms rolling off his tongue with ease, it’s no surprise that when Netflix, which acquired the rights to Roald Dahl’s literary estate five years ago, planned to make a Wonka-inspired game show Goffe was clearly top of their list to bring back.
	

	In “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” which launched on Sept. 23, he stars alongside his son Ben Goffe — also an actor who has appeared in “Artemis Fowl,” among other titles — as well as a host of new Oompa-Loompas. (Unlike in the original film, these Oompa-Loompas “come in all shapes and sizes now,” as the contestants are told during the show.). Also back is Wilder, albeit only his voice, which has been, somewhat controversially, recreated in AI with the blessing of his wife, Wilder himself having died in 2016.


	Over the course of nine episodes, viewers will see 12 contestants take part in a series of increasingly wacky challenges in the hopes of winning a “lifetime’s supply of money” (approximately $3 million, calculated as an annual six-figure salary over 30 years), all played out on Wonka-themed set pieces, including the famous elevator and, of course, the edible candy room, complete with chocolate waterfall.

	Ahead of “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket” launching, Goffe, now 77, spoke with Variety about how he came to work on the competition show, what it was like to step back into the world of Wonka — and his feelings at hearing Wilder’s voice recreated by AI.
	
	
		How did this come about? Did Netflix reach out to you?	

	Well, I just had a phone call from my agent in New York saying they want you in Netflix, talking about “Wonka.” [I said] “Being in ‘Wonka?’ That was a long time ago.” And they said “Yeah, they still want you.” So that’s how I got into it, and I really loved the new one.
	
		Once you knew it was a game show, were you wondering what that format might be?	

	I was wondering how is this going to happen. But after a couple of days, I got used to it. The contestants were in their own bubble, so when they came on, you just nodded to them, because they were trying to get answers from your face, how they’re doing. So we’re not giving anything away. I was really pleased — thrilled — this time to have my son with me, Ben. [He’s] 33 years of age, an Oompa-Loompa! 
	
		What was it like for him to step into that iconic role?	

	Well, he’s grown up with “Wonka” through me, and he loved the first one, and when [Netflix] said about Ben being in it, he jumped at the chance. “Yeah, yeah, I’m going to be an Oompa-Loompa,” you know, because he’s an actor. He’s done Shakespeare, many, many movies. 
	
		Did you give any give him any tips?	

	No. None whatsoever. I was an Oompa-Loompa. You’re the new one. Learn — on the job!
	
		What was it like for you stepping back into the world of “Wonka”?	

	It was bizarre, going into the studio, into the chocolate room, in fact. And it was all modern. They still had a river. They still had a waterfall. It was absolutely fantastic, it was. And the river — last time, it was just dirty water, it smelled because we were pouring real cream and real sugar into it, and with the hot lights, it was melting. It was melting, and poor Michael Böllner, who played Augustus Gloop [in th 1971 film], he had to fall in it when he was a kid. And they ask him now, “What was it like, Michael? What was the river like?” [In a German accent] “It vas stinky vater!” in his best German. But it was lovely. But unfortunately, he wasn’t there, it was just myself and my young son, who wasn’t there in the original.
	
		Did you keep anything from the set of the original film?	

	Mmmmmm, yes. I might have a golden ticket, a real one or two. My children’s inheritance.
	
		Would you have wanted to be a contestant on “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” if you weren’t part of the cast?	

	No. It was great being the Oompa-Loompa just watching them, because I knew what they were going to win, lose, what’s going to happen if they lost [a challenge]. Which is not good on some occasions.
	
	
		Did you ever think that the original film would have such a lasting impact that you’d still be revisiting that world so many years later?	

	I am still absolutely amazed how big it still is. I get to go and do conventions, mainly in the States, and people say, “Yeah, we loved it. We came out the theater, when we saw the new ones. We came out the theater, but we were still singing ‘Oompa-Loompa doompa dee do’ — your movie.” They loved it. But I was surprised how big it still was and still is! And I thank the people for keeping it alive. If it wasn’t for the fans, it’d be gone.
	
		This time round there seems to be more diversity among the Oompa-Loompas…	

	[These] Oompa-Loompas, they weren’t just short. We had one bodybuilder, big guy, a tall guy, three ladies, a small man, and Ben. It was wonderful to have this diverse [cast of] people.
	
		Netflix has also brought Gene Wilder’s voice back for the show with AI, which has prompted some discussion. Was it weird hearing his voice again after so many years?	

	Well, “weird” is not the word. It was lovely hearing his voice again, because I loved that man. He was a gentle, fantastic character, very funny, very, very kind, and to hear him in the show, I was so pleased that Netflix had done it. He is Mr. Wonka. He is Willy Wonka. Gene Wilder is Willy Wonka.
	
		Was it uncanny hearing him again, or is it just like he’s standing there?	

	It’s just him standing there. I did shed a tear when I first heard it, because I loved the man so much. But then I thought he wouldn’t want me to do that. He’d want me to be an Oompa-Loompa, get out there, do the job. Yeah, that that was Gene. He was a lovely, lovely man.
	
		Did you have a favorite moment of filming this new show?	

	Yes, the breaks! It was one of the best moments of my life to do “Wonka” again. I started my career on “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” and now I am pleased to announce to Variety that I’ve ended my career on “Willy Wonka’s The Golden Ticket.”

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

title: The Best Pop Culture Halloween Costumes for 2026: From Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Shrubs to Taylor Swift’s Knicks Shirt
description: Expect to see plenty of hockey jerseys, hospital scrubs and suspiciously elaborate shrubbery on the streets this Halloween. Some revelers will be ch
body:
Expect to see plenty of hockey jerseys, hospital scrubs and suspiciously elaborate shrubbery on the streets this Halloween. Some revelers will be channeling Ilya and Shane from “Heated Rivalry,” others will be pulling overnight shifts as the doctors of “The Pitt” — and the most committed friend groups may skip dressing as Bad Bunny altogether and show up as the bushes from his Super Bowl halftime show.

	As usual, the year’s biggest movies and TV shows provide a gold mine of costume inspiration. Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” offers a particularly cinematic couples costume in Zendaya’s Athena and Matt Damon’s Odysseus, while “KPop Demon Hunters” practically begs for a three-person HUNTR/X get-up. Elsewhere, “Off Campus,” “Backrooms,” “Euphoria” and “Widow’s Bay” offer options ranging from exceedingly easy to the kind of niche reference that will earn approving nods from fellow obsessives.


	Musicians, meanwhile, have supplied some of the year’s most immediately recognizable looks. Harry Styles’ tiny red shorts from the “Dance No More” video are destined for Halloween parties, while Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love” album cover offers another ready-made pop-star transformation. And for anyone whose costume philosophy is simply “more rhinestones,” there’s always Dolly Parton.

	Shop the best pop-culture Halloween costumes for 2026 below:
	
		 Nikki in ‘Obsession’	



	

									©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	Channel Inde Navarrette’s Nikki with the horror hit’s instantly recognizable red-and-black zebra halter, black bottoms and plenty of gold jewelry. Bonus points for a Willow prop — and a little fake blood if you want to take things in a more sinister direction.



			
			
			
			
	

	
					
	
		Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Bushes 	



	

									Christopher Polk/Billboard
	



	For one of the year’s most absurdly specific group costumes, skip dressing as Bad Bunny himself and go as the greenery surrounding him during his Super Bowl performance. All you really need is head-to-toe green, some faux foliage and friends willing to commit to the bit.


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Athena and Odysseus in ‘The Odyssey’	



	

									Melinda Sue Gordon
	



	Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” gives couples an elevated alternative to the standard toga costume: think weathered linen, leather and patinated bronze rather than pristine Grecian robes. Matt Damon’s battle-worn Odysseus and Zendaya’s draped, earth-toned Athena make an especially good pairing.


						
			
	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					
	
		‘Celebrity Row’ at MSG	



	

									Getty Images
	



	Sometimes the best celebrity costume is also the easiest: recreate Taylor Swift and her crew’s matching Stevie Nicks concert shirts for a group look that requires little more than merch, jeans and Swift-level enthusiasm. It’s niche enough to reward anyone who spent the year chronically online.


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Hannah and Garret in ‘Off Campus’	



	

									Liane Hentscher/Prime Video
	



	Prime Video’s buzzy hockey romance makes Hannah and Garrett an easy couples costume: she can channel Hannah’s signature campus looks while he throws on a Briar U hockey jersey. For a more overtly Halloween-ready option, recreate the show’s bunny-and-magician pairing.


						
			
	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Operatives in ‘Backrooms’	



	

									Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	Hazmat suits have rarely felt more zeitgeisty. Suit up in protective gear, respirators and utility equipment to become one of the operatives venturing into the fluorescent-lit nightmare of “Backrooms” — particularly effective if your entire friend group commits.


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Magick in ‘Euphoria’	



	

									Eddy Chen
	



	If your Halloween philosophy is “more is more,” Magick offers plenty to work with: dramatic makeup, maximalist styling and the kind of hyper-specific fashion choices that have always made “Euphoria” a costume gold mine. Consider it an excuse to pull out every rhinestone in your makeup drawer.


	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Ilya and Shane in ‘Heated Rivalry’	



	

									sabrina lantos
	



	The internet’s favorite hockey couple is practically made for a two-person costume. Go straightforward with rival hockey jerseys, or recreate one of Ilya and Shane’s more memorable off-ice looks for something that devoted “Heated Rivalry” fans will clock immediately.


						
			
	

	
					


	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					
	
		‘The Pitt’ Doctors 	



	

									Warrick Page/MAX
	



	Few costumes require less explaining — or shopping — than the doctors of “The Pitt.” Grab some medical scrubs, an ID badge and a stethoscope, then spend the evening looking appropriately exhausted for the full Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center effect.



	

	
					
	
		Dolly Parton 	



	

	



	Big blonde hair, bigger lashes, rhinestones and enough fringe to be visible from across the room: Dolly Parton remains one of pop culture’s most foolproof Halloween transformations. The trick is not to exercise restraint.


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Olivia Rodrigo Album Cover	



	

									Geffen
	



	Rodrigo’s third album offers a very 2026 costume for anyone looking beyond her already Halloween-friendly “Sour” and “Guts” eras. Recreate the cover’s styling and makeup, then carry around a mock vinyl sleeve in case anyone needs the reference spelled out.


						
			
	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Harry Styles in ‘Dance No More’ Music Video	



	

									YouTube
	



	Possibly the easiest excuse you’ll ever get to wear tiny red shorts on Halloween. Styles spends much of the “Dance No More” video dancing in custom Marc Jacobs short-shorts and sneakers, making the look both instantly recognizable and surprisingly simple to copy.


						
			
	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					
	
		Huntr/x in ‘Kpop Demon Hunters’	



	

									NETFLIX
	



	Rumi, Mira and Zoey are tailor-made for a three-person costume: colorful stagewear, pop-star hair and makeup and, naturally, demon-hunting accessories. Netflix has even released officially licensed HUNTR/X costumes, though the trio’s highly distinctive looks are ripe for DIY interpretations too.


			
			
			
			
	

	
					
	
		Patricia in ‘Widow’s Bay’	



	

									Apple TV
	



	Patricia’s distinctive “Widow’s Bay” look offers a more unexpected choice for anyone who wants their costume to inspire a few “wait, I know this” reactions. Nail the hair, wardrobe and character-specific accessories and let the year’s horror obsessives do the rest.

title: Ryan Murphy Says He ‘Just Finished the Script’ for a ‘Glee’ Reboot and Has Spoken to the Original Cast: ‘They All Were Very Enthusiastic’
description: It’s a good day to be a Gleek. Following long-swirling rumors of a potential “Glee” reboot, creator Ryan Murphy has officially weighed in and reveal
body:
It’s a good day to be a Gleek. Following long-swirling rumors of a potential “Glee” reboot, creator Ryan Murphy has officially weighed in and revealed that there’s a script.

	“Well, funny you ask, ’cause I just finished the script an hour ago,” Murphy told Entertainment Tonight on Wednesday. “So, we have a script. Brad [Falchuk], Ian [Brennan] and I, who wrote all the first two seasons, have written something. I’ve been in touch with around 10 of the original cast members. It’s very sweet, and they all had a lot of questions, but they all were very enthusiastic about the idea.”
	

	The news comes just a week after Lea Michele, who played Rachel Berry for all six seasons of the musical comedy, said that she’d be happy to return for a reboot. Speaking with E! News, she said, “I love ‘Glee.’ I will always love ‘Glee.’ I love Ryan Murphy. It just holds such a special place in my heart for me… I will follow Ryan wherever he goes.”


	Speaking of the reboot, Murphy noted that although there is a script, “nobody’s read it.” “So I don’t know, we’ll see,” he continued. “I vowed to myself that I wanted to write a couple of them to see what people think, particularly the cast, ’cause we were very close when we were making it.”

	“Glee” first premiered in Sept. 2009, and in addition to Michele, starred Corey Monteith, Naya Rivera, Dianna Agron, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Heather Morris, Chris Colfer and more.

body:
'Pioneer Woman' Ree Drummond
                          'Homeless' Foster Son Apparently Put Her Cell Down
                          After 2025 Assault Arrest For Biting Officer
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 23, 2026

            The son of 'Pioneer Woman' Ree Drummond faced legal trouble months before his arrest for assaulting a police officer and possession of drugs -- with the famous chef’s son also accused of biting an officer's hand last year ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Jamar Goff, who Ree began fostering in 2018, was accused of biting the hand of a detention or correctional officer in May 2025.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            At the time, Jamar said he was homeless and had just started working at McDonald's.
      

            It appears he listed a cell phone number connected to Ree as his family contact on the court paperwork. He didn’t list her name but said "foster parent."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Ree and Ladd Drummond's foster son was arrested this month in Alabama on charges related to an alleged assault on a police officer and drug possession.
      
    
            Jamar was booked into jail on September 15.
      
    
            The court docs said Jamar was found by an officer sleeping near a fountain without a shirt on at the University of Alabama. Cops say he told the officer he was waiting for someone to sell him "ice," which is a nickname for meth.
      
    
            The docs say the officer discovered Jamar had a warrant for his arrest and tried to put him in handcuffs ... but he allegedly ran and later allegedly struck an officer with his palm.
      
    
            Following his arrest, cops say they found a glass pipe and 1.8 grams of meth. Jamar’s bond was set at $37K. In the docs, Jamar said he was homeless.

title: 'Always Something There to Remind Me' Singer Peter Byrne Dead at 74
description:
Naked Eyes Vocalist Peter Byrne
                          Dead at 74 ...
body:
Naked Eyes Vocalist Peter Byrne
                          Dead at 74 ...
                          Sang 'Always Something There to Remind Me'
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Peter Byrne, who sang Naked Eyes hits "Always Something There to Remind Me" and "Promises, Promises," is dead.
      
    
            The singer-songwriter died Sept. 14 in Los Angeles after a brief illness ... according to Billboard. The band's manager told the outlet Peter died peacefully.
      
    
            Peter's official cause of death is unclear.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He began his music career way back in the mid-1970s ... he was in a duo with Jeff Starrs from 1976 to 1977 before joining the band Studio from 1977 to 1979.
      
    
            In 1982, Peter started Naked Eyes with close friend Rob Fisher, and they found instant success. Their debut album -- titled "Naked Eyes" in the USA and "Burning Bridges" in the UK -- charted on the Billboard 200.
      
    
            "Always Something There to Remind Me" -- a song from the debut album -- proved to be the group's biggest hit ... reaching #8 on the Billboard Hot 100.
      
    
            Their other hits include ... "(What) In the Name of Love," "When the Lights Go Out," and many more.
      
    
            Despite their radio hits, Peter and Rob only played together for a couple of years ... they disbanded in 1984, having never toured together. Rob died in 1999, and in 2006 Peter restarted the group.
      
    
            Peter is survived by his three children ... Merlin, Dylan, and Chloe.
      
    
            He was 74.
      
    
            RIP
